subject: chemistry
pattern: Electrochemistry carries about 7-8 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper: 1-mark definitions (molar conductivity, Faraday's law, salt bridge), 2-mark Kohlrausch law or Nernst numericals, 3-mark numericals (conductivity, Gibbs energy, Faraday) and batteries or fuel cell, and a 5-mark derivation of the Nernst equation or conductivity variation. Examiners expect cell notation, balanced half reactions and numericals with substitution and units.

questions.q: Define molar conductivity. Mention its SI unit.
questions.answer: Molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) of a solution at a given concentration is the conductance of the volume V of the solution containing one mole of the electrolyte kept between two electrodes of unit area of cross-section separated by unit distance. $\Lambda_m = \kappa/C$, or $\kappa \times 1000 / M$ in S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$. SI unit: S m$^2$ mol$^{-1}$.
keywords: conductance of solution containing one mole

questions.q: State Faraday's first law of electrolysis.
questions.answer: Faraday's first law: the amount of substance deposited or liberated at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity (charge) passed through the electrolyte. Mathematically $m = Z\,Q = Z\,I\,t$, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent, I the current in ampere and t the time in seconds.

questions.q: What is the function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
questions.answer: A salt bridge (a U-tube containing an inert electrolyte such as KCl or KNO$_3$ in agar-agar gel) completes the electrical circuit by allowing ions to move between the two half cells. It maintains electrical neutrality in both compartments and eliminates the liquid junction potential. The ions of the salt bridge have nearly equal ionic mobilities.

questions.q: State Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions. Mention one application.
questions.answer: Kohlrausch law: the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cations and anions, each multiplied by the number of ions present per formula unit of the electrolyte. $\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+\lambda_+^\circ + \nu_-\lambda_-^\circ$. Application: calculating $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of weak electrolytes such as acetic acid, and determining their degree of dissociation $\alpha = \Lambda_m / \Lambda_m^\circ$.

questions.q: Calculate the emf of the cell Zn | Zn$^{2+}$(0.1 M) || Cu$^{2+}$(0.01 M) | Cu at 298 K. ($E^\circ_{cell} = 1.10$ V)
questions.answer: Cell reaction: Zn + Cu$^{2+}$ $\to$ Zn$^{2+}$ + Cu, n = 2. Nernst equation: $E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{[Zn^{2+}]}{[Cu^{2+}]} = 1.10 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{0.1}{0.01} = 1.10 - 0.02955 \times 1 = 1.0705$ V. So the emf of the cell is approximately 1.07 V.

questions.q: Distinguish between primary and secondary cells with one example each.
questions.answer: Primary cell: the cell reaction is irreversible; the cell cannot be recharged and is discarded after use. Example: dry cell (Leclanche cell), mercury cell. Secondary cell: the cell reaction is reversible; it can be recharged by passing current in the opposite direction and used again and again. Example: lead storage battery, nickel-cadmium cell.

questions.q: Calculate the mass of copper deposited when a current of 2 A is passed through CuSO$_4$ solution for 30 minutes. (Molar mass of Cu = 63.5 g mol$^{-1}$, 1 F = 96500 C)
questions.answer: Charge Q = I t = 2 A $\times$ (30 $\times$ 60 s) = 3600 C. Cu$^{2+}$ + 2e$^-$ $\to$ Cu; 2 F = 193000 C deposits 63.5 g. Mass deposited = (63.5 / 193000) $\times$ 3600 = 1.184 g. Thus about 1.18 g of copper is deposited.

questions.q: Derive the relationship between standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant of a cell reaction.
questions.answer: The electrical work done by a reversible cell equals the decrease in Gibbs energy: $\Delta_rG = -nFE_{cell}$. Under standard conditions, $\Delta_rG^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$. Also, $\Delta_rG^\circ = -RT\ln K_c$. Equating both, $nFE^\circ_{cell} = RT\ln K_c$, so $E^\circ_{cell} = \dfrac{RT}{nF}\ln K_c$. At 298 K, converting to log, $E^\circ_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log K_c$. Thus equilibrium constant can be obtained from $E^\circ_{cell}$.

questions.q: Describe the construction of the lead storage battery. Write the anode, cathode and overall cell reactions during discharge.
questions.answer: Anode: lead plates; cathode: grid of lead packed with PbO$_2$; electrolyte: 38 percent H$_2$SO$_4$ by mass. During discharge: Anode: Pb(s) + SO$_4^{2-}$(aq) $\to$ PbSO$_4$(s) + 2e$^-$. Cathode: PbO$_2$(s) + SO$_4^{2-}$(aq) + 4H$^+$(aq) + 2e$^-$ $\to$ PbSO$_4$(s) + 2H$_2$O(l). Overall: Pb + PbO$_2$ + 2H$_2$SO$_4$ $\to$ 2PbSO$_4$ + 2H$_2$O. On recharging, the reaction is reversed.

questions.q: Calculate $\Lambda_m^\circ$ for acetic acid given $\Lambda_m^\circ$ (NaOAc) = 91.0, $\Lambda_m^\circ$ (HCl) = 426.2 and $\Lambda_m^\circ$ (NaCl) = 126.5 S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$.
questions.answer: By Kohlrausch law: $\Lambda_m^\circ$(CH$_3$COOH) = $\lambda^\circ$(CH$_3$COO$^-$) + $\lambda^\circ$(H$^+$). This equals $\Lambda_m^\circ$(NaOAc) + $\Lambda_m^\circ$(HCl) $-$ $\Lambda_m^\circ$(NaCl) = 91.0 + 426.2 $-$ 126.5 = 390.7 S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.q: The conductivity of 0.20 M KCl solution is 0.0248 S cm$^{-1}$. Calculate its molar conductivity.
questions.answer: Molar conductivity $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{M}$, where $\kappa$ is the conductivity in S cm$^{-1}$ and M the molarity. $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{0.0248 \times 1000}{0.20} = 124$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.q: What is a fuel cell? Write the electrode reactions in the H$_2$-O$_2$ fuel cell and mention two advantages.
questions.answer: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell that converts the chemical energy of a fuel (such as H$_2$) directly into electrical energy, with reactants supplied continuously. Anode: 2H$_2$(g) + 4OH$^-$(aq) $\to$ 4H$_2$O(l) + 4e$^-$. Cathode: O$_2$(g) + 2H$_2$O(l) + 4e$^-$ $\to$ 4OH$^-$(aq). Overall: 2H$_2$ + O$_2$ $\to$ 2H$_2$O. Advantages: high efficiency (about 70 percent), non-polluting (product is water), continuous operation.

questions.q: Derive the Nernst equation for the electrode potential of an electrode M$^{n+}$/M and for the emf of a cell.
questions.answer: For the reduction M$^{n+}$(aq) + ne$^-$ $\to$ M(s), $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$, where $Q = \dfrac{[M]}{[M^{n+}]} = \dfrac{1}{[M^{n+}]}$. Since $\Delta G = -nFE$ and $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$: $-nFE = -nFE^\circ + RT\ln\dfrac{1}{[M^{n+}]}$. Dividing by $-nF$, $E = E^\circ - \dfrac{RT}{nF}\ln\dfrac{1}{[M^{n+}]} = E^\circ + \dfrac{RT}{nF}\ln[M^{n+}]$. At 298 K, $E_{M^{n+}/M} = E^\circ + \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log[M^{n+}]$. For a cell reaction aA + bB $\to$ cC + dD: $E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$.
keywords: delta G = delta G0 + RT ln Q

questions.q: Explain the variation of molar conductivity with concentration for strong and weak electrolytes. How is $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of a strong electrolyte determined?
questions.answer: Molar conductivity increases on dilution for both types of electrolyte, because the volume containing one mole increases. Strong electrolytes: they are completely ionised; on dilution, interionic attractions decrease and ionic mobility increases, so $\Lambda_m$ rises slowly and linearly with $\sqrt{c}$ (Debye-Huckel-Onsager equation): $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$. Extrapolating the straight line plot of $\Lambda_m$ against $\sqrt{c}$ to zero concentration gives $\Lambda_m^\circ$ (intercept), and the slope is $-A$. Weak electrolytes: at higher concentration, ionisation is small so $\Lambda_m$ is low; on dilution, the degree of dissociation increases sharply, so $\Lambda_m$ rises steeply at low concentration and the plot cannot be extrapolated, hence $\Lambda_m^\circ$ is obtained using Kohlrausch law.
